(p-188) Sūrat al-Wāqi'a

﴿When the Event befalls﴾. That is: when the Resurrection comes about, and that is at the second blast (al-nafkha al-thāniya). The expression of it as "the Event" (al-wāqi'a) serves to announce that its befalling is certain without doubt, as if it were an event in itself, apart from the falling that occurs within the scope of the condition. It is as if it were said: "what is to occur has occurred, and what is to happen has happened." The "idhā" (when) is governed by an implied verb that indicates awe and dreadfulness, as if it were said: "When the Event befalls, there will be from the terrors what no speech can express." And it has been said: it is governed by the negation understood from the words of the Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 2:

﴿There is no denying its occurrence.﴾ That is: when it occurs, there will be no soul that lies about God Most High, or lies in denying it as it lies today. The lam here is like the lam in His saying, Most High: ﴿Oh, would that I had sent forth for my life!﴾ This sentence, according to the first interpretation, is an interjection (i'tiraD, parenthetical clause) confirming the content of the conditional, on the basis that kadhibah is a verbal noun like ʿafiyah, meaning: there is no lying, at all, concerning its occurrence or regarding it; rather, everything that has been reported about it is true and truthful, without any doubt.

Its statement, ﴿abasing, exalting﴾, is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is abasing some people and exalting others. This is an affirmation of its greatness and a declaration of its awesomeness, for great events are of this nature. Or it is an explanation of what will happen on that day: the abasement of the wretched to the lowest depths and the elevation of the blessed to the high ranks; and the shaking of things and the removal of celestial bodies from their places, by the scattering of the stars, the falling of the heaven in pieces, and the moving of the mountains through the air like clouds. The placing of "abasing" before "exalting" serves to intensify the awesomeness. It has also been read as "abasing, exalting" in the accusative, as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of "the Event" (al-Wāqi'ah).

"And His saying, ﴿When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking﴾: that is, it is convulsed with a severe convulsion, such that whatever is upon it of buildings and mountains collapses. It is connected to "bringing low, raising high" — that is, it brings low and raises up at the time the earth is shaken, for at that time what is high is lowered and what is low is raised. Or it is a substitution (badal) for "when the Event occurs."

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿And the mountains will be crumbled, crumbled﴾ — the verse is 56:5, but the passage quotes it as given.

"And the mountains will be crumbled to dust" — that is, they will be ground up until they become like ground, kneaded sawiq (a fine flour of parched grain), from the verb basta al-sawiq, meaning he kneaded the sawiq (sawiq: parched grain flour) when he moistened it; or they will be driven and set moving from their places, from basta al-ghanam, meaning he drove the sheep, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the mountains will be set in motion﴾. It is also read "rujjat" and "bussat," meaning: they will be shaken and will go away.

﴿Fa-kānat﴾ i.e., "then it became," as a result of that.

﴿habā'an﴾ dust.

﴿munbaththan﴾ scattered.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 7:

﴿And you shall be﴾ either an address to the present community and the earlier nations, by way of prevailing (taghlib), or an address to the present community alone.

﴿Kinds (azwaj)﴾ i.e., categories (asnaf).

﴿Three﴾ Each category is, in existence or in mention, paired with another category, and so it is a pair (zawj).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verses 8–9:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So the companions of the right hand—what are the companions of the right hand?﴾ ﴿And the companions of the left hand—what are the companions of the left hand?﴾ is a division and classification of the three pairs (of groups), together with a general indication of their states before their detailed explanation. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So the companions of the right hand﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and His saying: ﴿what are the companions of the right hand﴾ is its predicate (khabar), with the interrogative "ma" being a second subject (mubtada' thani), what follows it being its predicate, and the whole sentence being the predicate of the first. The original form is "ma hum?" (what are they?), i.e., what are they in their condition and attribute? Although "ma" is commonly used to seek the concept of a name and reality, it may also be used to seek an attribute or state. You say: "Ma Zayd?" (What is Zayd?), and it is answered: "He is a scholar or a physician." Placing the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is because it is more effective in magnifying (the matter). The same applies to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the companions of the left hand—what are the companions of the left hand?﴾. The intended meaning is to make the listener marvel at the condition of the two groups in grandeur and dreadfulness, as if it were said: "The companions of the right hand are in the utmost good state, and the companions of the left hand are in the utmost evil state." People have spoken about the two groups: it was said, "The companions of the right hand are the people of the lofty station, and the companions of the left hand are the people of the base station," taking this from their being blessed with the right-hand side and their being regarded as ill-omened by the left-hand side. It was said, "They are those whose records are given to them in their right hands, and those whose records are given to them in their left hands." It was said, "They are those who are taken to the Garden by the right side, and those who are taken to the Fire by the left side." It was said, "(They are) the companions of the right and the companions of ill omen," for the blessed are blessed (mayamin) for themselves through their obedience, and the wretched are ill-omened (masha'im) for themselves through their disobedience.

The statement of God Most High, ﴿And the foremost, the foremost﴾, is the third of the three categories of spouses. Perhaps their mention is delayed, although they are the most excellent and the first of the categories in virtue, so that their mention is joined with the explanation of the admirable qualities of their conditions. Moreover, presenting them under the title of "foremost" without qualification indicates that they have seized the prize of precedence in every respect.

Scholars have also spoken about them. It was said: they are those who hastened to faith and obedience when the truth became manifest, without hesitation or delay. It was said: they are those who excelled in acquiring virtues and perfections. It was said: they are those who prayed towards both qiblahs, as God Most High said: ﴿And the foremost, the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers﴾. It was said: they are those who hastened to the five daily prayers. It was said: they are those who race to good deeds. Whatever the case, the sentence is a subject and predicate (mubtada' wa khabar), and the meaning is: "And the foremost are those whose conditions are well known and whose excellences are recognized," like the saying of Abu al-Najm: [I am Abu al-Najm, and my poetry is my poetry]. In this there is the magnification of their status, and the announcement that their excellence is widespread, and their independence from being described with praise, which is not hidden. It was said: "And the foremost to the obedience of God Most High" are the foremost to His mercy, or the foremost to goodness, and the foremost to Paradise.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 11:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the foremost (al-sabiqun), and the distance implied in it, despite the recency of what is pointed to, serves to indicate the elevated rank of those people in excellence. Its position in i'rab (grammatical analysis) is nominative, as a mubtada' (subject), and its khabar (predicate) is what follows it, meaning: those described by that sublime attribute.

﴿The foremost (al-muqarrabun)﴾ means: those whose ranks were brought near to the Mighty Throne, whose degrees were raised and whose stations were elevated, and whose pure souls ascended to the sanctuaries of holiness. This is the most apparent and best-known view regarding the i'rab of these sentences. What the eloquence of the revelation requires is that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So the companions of the right﴾ is the khabar of an elided mubtada', and likewise His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and the companions of the left﴾, and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and the foremost﴾. This is because, when the division of people into the three categories is being explained, what is expected is an explanation of the three categories themselves; as for their attributes and conditions, the proper course is that they be explained afterwards, by attributing them to those categories. The sense is: one of them is the companions of the right, the other is the companions of the left, and the third is the foremost. The difference is that, since the explanation of the conditions of the first two categories was postponed, each of them is followed by a parenthetical sentence placed between the two categories, which informs in a general way of the extremes to which their conditions reach, in good and in evil, indicating that each of their conditions has a detailed explanation yet to come. However, this is not on the basis that the interrogative "ma" (ما) is a mubtada' with what follows it as its khabar, as Sibawayh held in such constructions. Rather, it is on the basis that it is a khabar for what follows it, since the core of the benefit lies in showing that the companions of the right are a wondrous matter, as the fact that "ma" is a khabar conveys, whereas if it were a mubtada' it would convey that a wondrous matter is the companions of the right. The same applies to "the companions of the left." As for the last category, since the explanation of the excellent qualities of its condition is joined to its mention, there was no need to introduce a model (unmudhaj) before it. So His saying, exalted is He, ﴿the foremost﴾ is a mubtada', and the explicit noun is used in place of the pronoun (al-izhar fi maqam al-idmar) for the sake of magnification. And "those" (ulaika) is a second mubtada' or an apposition (badal) to the first, and what follows it is its khabar, or the second is the khabar, and the whole sentence is the khabar of the first.

"And His saying: ﴿in Gardens of Bliss﴾ is connected to "al-muqarrabun" (those brought near), or to an implied verb which is a circumstantial clause (hal) from its pronoun, i.e., "being in Gardens of Bliss." It was also said: it is a second predicate (khabar thani) of the demonstrative (ism al-isharah). In this there is an objection: informing that they are "brought near" does not add any further distinction. And it has been recited as "fi jannati al-na'im" (in the Garden of Bliss)."

**Thulla min al-awwalin** (﻿﴿A multitude from the earlier peoples﴾) is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are a numerous community (ummah jammah) from the earlier peoples, namely the bygone nations from the time of Adam until our Prophet, upon whom be the best of prayers and peace, and upon the great prophets who came between them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 14:

﴿And a few from the later generations.﴾ That is: from this Ummah. It is not contradicted by the words of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Indeed my Ummah will be more numerous than [all] the other nations." For the fact that the foremost (sabiqun) of the earlier nations are more numerous than the foremost of this Ummah does not prevent the followers (tabi'un) of these from being more numerous than the followers of those. Nor is it refuted by His words, Exalted is He: ﴿for the companions of the right hand﴾ ﴿a multitude from the earlier generations﴾ ﴿and a multitude from the later generations﴾, because the multitude of each of the two groups in themselves does not contradict the majority of one of them over the other. It will come that two-thirds [of the people of Paradise] are from this Ummah. It has also been related with a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) chain that "the earlier and the later" here also refers to the earlier and later members of this Ummah. The derivation of thullah (multitude) is from ith-thil, which means breaking.

Reclining on them, facing one another. These are two circumstantial clauses (ḥālān) referring back to the pronoun hidden in the predicate that is attached to "upon couches," meaning: settled upon couches, reclining on them, facing one another, not looking at one another from the backs of their necks. This is a description of them as having good companionship and refined manners and etiquette.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 17:

﴿Yatūfu ʿalayhim﴾ is another circumstantial clause (ḥāl) or a resumptive new sentence (istiʾnāf), meaning: they go around them (yadūru ḥawlahum) for service (lil-khidmah).

﴿Wildānun mukhalladūn﴾: that is, they remain forever (mubqawna abadan) in the form of youths (ʿalā shakl al-wildān) and their freshness (ṭarawātihim), not changing from it. It was also said: they are wearing earrings (muqarraṭūn), and al-khuld means al-qirṭ (earring). It was said: they are the children of the people of this world who had neither good deeds for which they would be rewarded nor evil deeds for which they would be punished. With cups (بِأكْوابٍ) — vessels without handles or spouts.

And pitchers (وَأبارِيقَ) — that is, vessels with handles and spouts.

And a cup from a flowing spring (وَكَأْسٍ مِن مَعِينٍ) — that is, wine flowing from springs. It has been said that the singular "cup" (kas) is used here because a vessel is only called a kas when it is full.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 19:

﴿They will not be affected with headache by it﴾. That is, because of it. Its literal sense is that their headache does not proceed from it. It has also been read "lā yuṣaddaʿūna" (they will not be affected with headache), meaning: they will not become split apart or scattered, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On that Day they will be split apart﴾. It has also been read "lā yaṣṣaddaʿūna," meaning: some of them will not separate others from one another.

﴿And they will not be drained of their reason﴾. That is, they will not become intoxicated, from anzafa al-shārib, when a drinker's intellect or his drink is exhausted.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 20:

﴿And fruit of what they choose﴾. That is: they select it, and "they take" its best and finest part.
And the flesh of birds, of whatever they desire. That is, whatever they wish for. It is also read "wa-luhumi ṭayrin" (with the plural "luhūm").

(p-192) ﴿And wide-eyed maidens (ḥūrun ʿīn)﴾ with the nominative (rafʿ) is either coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon "wildān" (youths), or it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, meaning: "therein, or for them, are wide-eyed maidens." It has also been read in the genitive (jarr), coordinated upon "gardens of bliss" (jannāt al-naʿīm), as if it were said: "They are in gardens, and fruit, and meat, and the company of wide-eyed maidens." Or it is coordinated upon "cups" (akwāb), because the meaning of "youths of everlasting youth will circulate among them with cups" is: "they are made to enjoy cups and..." [the text reads: "they are made to enjoy with cups and"]. And with the accusative (naṣb), meaning: "and they will be given wide-eyed maidens."
﴿like preserved pearls﴾ is either an adjectival qualifier (ṣifah) of "ḥūr," or a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl).

﴿A reward for what they used to do﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning: He does this to them as a reward for their deeds. Or it is an emphatic infinitive absolute (masdar mu'akkid), meaning: they are rewarded with a reward.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 25:

﴿They hear therein no idle talk﴾ i.e., falsehood (batilan).

﴿Nor any sinful speech﴾ i.e., and "nor" (wa-la) is taken as relating to sin (ithm), meaning: there is no idle talk therein, nor any sinful speech, nor any hearing [of such], as in his saying:

*"Nor do you see the dhabb lizard therein entering its burrow"*

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 26:

﴿Illa qilā﴾ i.e., qawlan (a saying).

﴿salāman salāman﴾ is an apposition (badal) for qīlan, like His statement, exalted is He: ﴿They hear therein no idle talk, nor any sin, but only the saying: "Peace, peace."﴾ Or it is its attribute (sifah), or its object (maf'ul), in the sense of: "They hear therein nothing except that they say: 'Peace, peace.'" The meaning is that they spread the greeting of peace, so they greet one another with peace after peace; or that each of the one who greets and the one greeted hears nothing from the other except the other's greeting of peace, either initiating it or returning it. It has also been read as "salāmun salāmun" by way of hikayah (quotation).

"And the companions of the right" — this opens the detailed account of the fortunate ones among them, whose affairs were summarized at the division (of people into groups), following the detailed account of the affairs of the foremost (al-sabiqun). It is the subject (mubtada').

The phrase ﴿What are the companions of the right?﴾ is an interrogative clause, brought to magnify them and to express amazement at their condition. You have already learned how it is composed. Its position (i'rab) is either in the nominative case, as the predicate (khabar) of the subject, or it is a parenthetical clause (mu'taridah) with no position in the sentence. The predicate (khabar) is the statement of Allah, the Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 28:

﴿In lote-trees without thorns﴾. And this, according to the first view, is a second predicate of the subject, or a predicate of an omitted subject. The sentence is a resumptive statement (istinaf) explaining what was left vague in God's words, ﴿What are the companions of the right?﴾, regarding their exalted rank. That is, they are in lote-trees without thorns, unlike the lote-trees of this world, which is the nabq tree (jujube), as if its thorns had been cut off (khudda), i.e., removed. It was also said: "makhdud" means its branches are bent (mathniyy) because of the abundance of its fruit, from the verb khadada al-ghusn, meaning he bent the branch while it was still green (ratb).

﴿And talh (acacia) arranged in tiers﴾. Its fruit is arranged in layers from its bottom to its top, and it has no visible trunk. It is the banana tree and Umm Ghaylan, and it has many well-ordered, fragrant blossoms. On the authority of al-Suddi: it is a tree that resembles the talh of this world, but it has fruit sweeter than honey. On the authority of Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that he recited "wa-ṭalʿin" (﻿وَطَلْعٍ, "and spathe") and said: "What is the matter with the talh?" He recited His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For it is a spathe arranged in tiers﴾. It was said: "Shall we change it?" He said: "The verses of the Qur'an are not to be disturbed or altered." On the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, the same.
And ﴿a shade extended﴾: stretched out and spread wide, neither contracting nor being overtaken, like the shade between the break of dawn and the rising of the sun.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 31:

﴿And flowing water⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿ —﻿﻿ that is poured out for them wherever they wish and however they desire, without toil⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿ — or poured water, flowing on the ground without a trench.﻿﻿ It is as if [this] depicts the state of the foremost (al-sabiqun) in the most splendid form conceivable to city-dwellers, while [the phrase] "the companions of the right" [describes their state] in the most perfect form conceivable to people of the desert, signalling that the two states are complementary.
﴿And fruit in abundance﴾, according to the varieties and kinds.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 33:

﴿Neither cut off﴾ at any time, as the fruits of this world are cut off.

﴿Nor forbidden﴾ to those who partake of them in any manner; they are not restricted for them as the gardens of this world are restricted. It has been read as "fakihatun kathirah" (abundant fruit) in the nominative (bi'l-raf'), upon the reading "wa-hunaka fakihah" (and there is fruit there), etc., like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [there are] wide-eyed maidens﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 34:

﴿And couches raised high﴾. That is: of elevated rank; or arranged in layers and raised up; or raised upon bedsteads. It has also been said: "the furush (couches)" are the women, where "bedding" (firash) is used as a metaphor for the woman, and their being raised high refers to their being upon adorned couches (arara'ik). God Most High says: ﴿They and their spouses, in shade, reclining upon couches﴾. And what the words of God Most High indicate is confirmed by this:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 35:

﴿Indeed, We have produced them with a (special) production.﴾ According to the first interpretation, a pronoun referring to the women is left implicit (ahmara), its reference being clearly indicated by the mention of the furush (couches), which are the beds (al-madajie), so that the meaning is plainly understood. The sense is: We began their creation anew, a fresh beginning, or We originated them without birth, a bringing into being or a re-creation. In a hadith: "They are those who passed away in the worldly abode as old women, white-haired and blear-eyed; Allah the Exalted made them, after their old age, of equal age (atrab), of one and the same age in youthfulness, so that whenever their husbands come to them, they find them as virgins (abkar)."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 56, verses 36–37:**

﴿We have made them virgins﴾, and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿loving, of equal age﴾. ﴿Uruban﴾ is the plural of ʿarūb (the one who shows affection to her husband and is good in conjugal submission (tabaʿhul)). It is also recited as ʿurban, with the rā' pronounced with a sukūn.

﴿Atraban﴾: equal in age, daughters of thirty-three years, and likewise their husbands.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 56, verses 36–37:**

﴿We have made them virgins﴾, and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿loving, of equal age﴾. ﴿Uruban﴾ is the plural of ʿarūb (the one who shows affection to her husband and is good in conjugal submission (tabaʿhul)). It is also recited as ʿurban, with the rā' pronounced with a sukūn.

﴿Atraban﴾: equal in age, daughters of thirty-three years, and likewise their husbands.

The lām in His words, exalted is He, ﴿for the companions of the right﴾ is connected either to "anshaʾnā" (We created), or "jaʿalnā" (We made), or to "atrāban" (equals in age), as in your saying: "This is a tirb (peer) of this," meaning: his equal in age. It was also said that it is connected to a omitted (verbal or prepositional) element that serves as a description of "abkāran" (virgins), meaning: existing for the companions of the right. Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they belong to the companions of the right. It was also said that it is the predicate of His words, exalted is He,

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 39–40:

﴿A throng from the earlier peoples﴾ ﴿and a throng from the later peoples﴾. This is far-fetched; rather, it is the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada'), with which the account of the People of the Right (ashab al-yamin) is concluded. That is: they are a community from the earlier peoples and a community from the later peoples. The discussion of these two phrases has already passed.

It is related from Abu al-'Aliyah, Mujahid, 'Ata' and al-Dahhak that "a throng from the earlier peoples" means from the foremost (sabiqun) of this Ummah, and "a throng from the later peoples" means from this Ummah at the end of time.

It is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, regarding this verse, that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "They are all from my Ummah."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 39–40:

﴿A throng from the earlier peoples﴾ ﴿and a throng from the later peoples﴾. This is far-fetched; rather, it is the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada'), with which the account of the People of the Right (ashab al-yamin) is concluded. That is: they are a community from the earlier peoples and a community from the later peoples. The discussion of these two phrases has already passed.

It is related from Abu al-'Aliyah, Mujahid, 'Ata' and al-Dahhak that "a throng from the earlier peoples" means from the foremost (sabiqun) of this Ummah, and "a throng from the later peoples" means from this Ummah at the end of time.

It is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, regarding this verse, that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "They are all from my Ummah."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 41:

﴿And the companions of the left﴾: this begins the detailing of their states, which were alluded to, when the division was made, with reference to their terror and horror, after the detailing of the good state of the companions of the right (aṣḥāb al-yamīn). The discussion of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿What are the companions of the left?﴾ is the very same as what was detailed in its counterpart, and likewise in His, may He be exalted, saying:

Qur'an 56:42: "In scorching wind and boiling water."

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary: "Samum" is the heat of fire that penetrates the pores (al-masam), and "hamim" is water that has reached the utmost degree of heat.
﴿And a shade of black smoke﴾: from a smoke that is intensely black.

ßﷺ

"Not cool" like other shades.

"Nor generous" — in which there is the good of the whole; it is called a shade, and then its two attributes are negated: coolness and generosity, by which is expressed the removal of the harm of heat, to establish that it is not a shade at all. It was also read "lā bāridun wa-lā karīmun" with nominative endings, meaning: it is neither cool nor generous.

The saying of Him, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, they were before that affluent﴾ is a reason (ta'lil) for their being afflicted with the punishment that has been mentioned. That is: indeed, they were before the mentioned evil punishment in the world, enjoying (mun'amin) every kind of blessing—of foods, drinks, good dwellings and noble abodes—immersed (munhamikin) in desires; so, inevitably, they were punished (ʿuwwidhu) with their opposites. (p-195)

ﷻ "And they used to persist in the great violation," i.e., the great sin, which is shirk (associating partners with God). From this comes their saying: "The boy reached the age of ḥinth," i.e., the age of puberty (ḥulm), and the time of being held accountable for sin.

Translation:

﴿And they used to say﴾ — due to the extreme of their insolence and obstinacy.

﴿Shall we, when we have died and become dust and bones?﴾ That is: some of our parts, the flesh and skin, had become dust, and some of them were decayed bones (ʿiẓām nakhiratan). The mention of dust first is because it is the most deeply rooted (ʿarāqa) in the matter of their disbelief in resurrection (istib'ād), and because it is the transformation of the parts that are visible (al-ajzāʾ al-bādiya). The word "idhā" (when) is purely temporal (mutamaḥḥiḍatun li-l-ẓarfiyya), and its governing element (al-ʿāmil fīhā) is what is indicated by the words of God Most High: ﴿Indeed, are we truly to be resurrected?﴾, not the same expression itself, because what follows "inna" (indeed), the lām (of emphasis) and the hamza (interrogative) does not govern what precedes them. The governing verb is nubʿathu (we are raised), and it is the referent of the denial. Restricting it to the stated time does not mean that their denial is specific to it, for they deny revival after death even if the body is in its own state; rather, it is to strengthen the denial of resurrection by directing it at a state wholly incompatible with it. The repetition of the hamza is to emphasise the rejection, and adorning the sentence with "inna" is to emphasise the denial, not a denial of the emphasis, as might be suspected from the apparent wording. The fronting of the hamza is because it requires initial position (al-ṣadāra), as in the words "Will you not then reason?" (afa-lā taʿqilūn), according to the view of the majority, for its meaning for them is the consequence of the denial, not the denial of the consequence, as is well known. The basis of their denial is not that they were actually established as resurrected while being dust and bones, but rather that they were liable to that and prepared for it; its referent is the denial of resurrection after that state. In this there is an indication of their extreme disbelief and persistence in error that cannot be surpassed.

The repetition of the interrogative hamza in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Or our fathers, the earliest ones?﴾ serves to emphasize the denial. The waw (and) is for conjunction with the pronoun hidden in "لَمَبْعُوثُونَ" (we shall indeed be raised, "lamab'uthun"), and the separation by the interrogative hamza makes that conjunction acceptable. They mean that the raising of their earliest forefathers is even more remote from occurring. It is also read as "أوْ آباؤُنا" (aw ʾābāʾunā, "or our fathers").

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 49:

﴿Say﴾ as a rebuttal of their denial and an affirmation of the truth.

﴿Indeed, the former peoples and the latter﴾ from among the nations, of whom you and your forefathers are part. In placing "the former" first there is an emphasis in the rebuttal, since their denial of the resurrection of their forefathers was stronger than their denial of their own resurrection, while observing the existential (wujudi) order.

(Surely) they will be gathered together (لَمَجْمُوعُونَ) after the resurrection (al-ba'th). It is also read as "لَمُجْمَعُونَ".

﴿Until the appointed time of a known day﴾: until the known day to which the world has been appointed, the genitive construction here being in the sense of "from" (min), as in "a ring of silver" (khatam fiddah).

﴿Then indeed you, O you who go astray﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon "indeed the first ones," which falls under the saying (al-qawl), and "ثُمَّ" (thumma, "then") indicates sequence either in time or in rank.

﴿the deniers﴾: that is, of the Resurrection (al-baʿth), and the address is to the people of Makkah and their like.

(p-196)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 52:

﴿La-ākilūna﴾ after the resurrection, the gathering, and the entry into Jahannam.

﴿min shajarin min zaqqūm﴾ The first "min" (min) is for the beginning of the limit (li-ibtida' al-ghayah), and the second is for explaining the tree and specifying it, meaning: you will be beginning to eat from a tree that is zaqqūm. It is also said that the second "min" is connected to an implied element, which is a description of "shajar" (tree), meaning: existing from zaqqūm.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 53:

﴿Then you will fill your bellies with it.﴾ That is: your bellies, from the intensity of hunger.

﴿Then you will drink upon it﴾ immediately after that, without delay, ﴿from the boiling water﴾, meaning water that is extremely hot. The feminine form of the pronoun referring to the tree, "الشجر" (al-shajar), appears first and the masculine form second, in accordance with meaning and wording. It is also read as "مِن شَجَرَةٍ" (min shajaratin, "from a tree"), in which case the pronoun in "عَلَيْهِ" (ʿalayhi, "upon it") refers to the zaqqum. It was also said that it refers to the one who eats.

God Almighty says: ﴿So you will drink like thirsty camels drink﴾. This serves as an elucidation of what precedes it, in the manner of His saying: ﴿So they denied Our servant﴾. That is: your drinking will not be ordinary drinking, but will be like the drinking of hīm (ṣ). The hīm are camels afflicted with al-huyām (ṣ), a disease that strikes them so that they drink and are never quenched. It is the plural of ahyam and haymā'. It is also said that al-hīm means the sands, on the basis that it is the plural of al-hayām, with a fatha on the ha', which is sand that does not hold together; it was pluralized on the pattern fu'ul, like saḥāb and suḥub, then it was lightened and what was done to the plural of abyad was done to it.

The meaning is that He will impose upon them, from hunger and the burning of the Fire in their bowels, what compels them to eat the zaqqūm (ṣ), which is like molten metal (al-muhl), and when they have filled their bellies with it, while it is at the extreme of heat and bitterness, He will impose upon them, from thirst, what compels them to drink the ḥamīm (ṣ), which cuts their intestines to pieces; so they drink as thirsty camels drink.

It has also been read as "shurba al-hīm" with a fatha, and that is likewise a verbal noun (maṣdar). It has been read with a kasra, on the basis that it is the name of what is drunk.

This is the nuzul of their [the wrongdoers'] ... [Note: the passage begins mid-argument.]

﴿This﴾ is what was mentioned of the kinds of punishment.

﴿This is their welcome on the Day of Judgment﴾, i.e., the Day of Recompense. If this is their nuzul, which is what is prepared for a guest from what is at hand, then consider what awaits them after they have settled in their abode and found rest in the Fire. There is in this a mockery of them that is not hidden. It has also been read as "nuzluhum" with the za' sukun for lightness. The sentence is directed from Him, exalted is He, by way of summation (fadhlaka), confirming the content of the preceding speech that was taught, and it is not included under the saying.

Notes on terms:
- Nuzul (a welcome or prepared provision for a guest).
- Fadhlaka (a concluding summary sentence, a conclusive remark).

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 57:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We created you, so why do you not believe?﴾ is a shift in address (talwin al-khitab) and a turning of it toward the disbelievers by way of rebuke and reproach (al-iljam wa al-tabkit). The fa' (fa, "so") is for the ordering (tartib) of the exhortation (tahdid) upon what precedes it, meaning: "Then why do you not believe in the creation? For what knowledge does not establish, and does not support, but rather points to the opposite of it, has nothing to do with belief whatsoever." It has also been said that it refers to belief in the Resurrection (al-ba'th), taking the act of origination (al-insha') as evidence for it, for whoever is able to originate is certainly able to restore. The first (interpretation) is the correct one, as you will come to understand in detail.(p-197)

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on surah 56, verse 58:

﴿Have you then considered that which you emit?﴾ That is: that which you eject into the wombs of the drops of semen. It has also been read with a fathah on the tā' (تَمْنُونَ, tamnūna, from manā, "to emit"), meaning: that which you emit (amnāhā).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 59:

﴿Do you create it?﴾ That is: do you determine it and shape it as a complete human being?

﴿Or are We the Creators?﴾ of it, without anything having any part in it. As for "am" (أم, or), it has been said that it is disjunctive (munqati'ah), because what follows it is a full sentence; so the meaning is: "Rather, are We the Creators?", with the interrogative being for confirmation (taqrir). It has also been said that it is conjunctive (muttasilah), and the coming of "al-Khaliqun" (the Creators) after "Nahnu" (We) is by way of emphasis (ta'kid), not by way of it being a predicate in its own right.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 60:

﴿We have decreed death among you﴾ i.e., We have apportioned it among you, and We have fixed the death of every person at a specific time, as Our will, which is founded upon far-reaching wisdoms, requires. And it has been read as "qadarna" (with the letter dal lightened, i.e., qadarna rather than qaddarna).

﴿And We are not to be outdone﴾ i.e., We are able [to do so].

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 61:

﴿Upon that We replace your likenesses﴾ No one can overcome Us in that We cause you to pass away and bring in place of you others like you from creation.

﴿And produce you in what you do not know﴾ of creation and its stages, and you will know the like of it. Al-Hasan (may Allah have mercy on him) said: That is, We will make you apes and swine. It has also been said: The meaning is: And We will produce you in the Resurrection in forms other than your forms in this world, and one whose affair is this, how could He be unable to bring you back? It has also been said: The meaning is: No one outstrips Us so as to flee from death or change its time. And "upon that We replace..." etc. is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the subject of "We have decreed" (qaddarnā), or a causal clause (ʿilla) for the decree, with "ʿalā" in the sense of "lām," and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (iʿtirāḍ).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 62:

﴿And you have certainly known the first creation﴾: it is their creation from a drop (nutfah), then from a clinging clot ('alaqah), then from a lump of flesh (mudghah). It has also been said: it is the original creation of Adam, peace be upon him, from dust.

﴿Then why do you not remember?﴾ That is, why do you not then remember that He who was capable of the first creation is certainly capable of the other creation (al-nash'ah al-ukhra)? For it is less in workmanship, given the availability of the materials, the specification of the parts, and the prior existence of the pattern. In this there is evidence for the validity of analogical reasoning (qiyas). It has also been read as "fa-lawla tadhkurun" from the triliteral root (dhakara). And in a report: "Extremely strange is the case of the one who denies the last creation while he sees the first creation, and strange is the case of the one who believes in the last creation while he strives for the abode of delusion."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 63:

﴿Have you then considered what you sow?﴾ That is: you scatter its seed and work in its land.

﴿Is it you who cause it to grow?﴾ That is, you make it sprout and bring it forth as a plant that is ﴾يَرِفُّ﴿ (yarif, that is, fresh and flourishing).

﴿Or are We the ones who cause it to grow?﴾ That is, the ones who cause it to sprout, not you. The discussion of the particle ﴾أمْ﴿ (am, "or," introducing an alternative question) is as has been mentioned just above.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 65:

﴿If We willed, We would have made it debris﴾: dry, crumbled, broken into pieces, after We had caused it to grow, and it had reached the state where you were eager to gather its produce.

(p-198) ﴿Then you would be left﴾: as a result of that.

﴿Lamenting﴾ (tafakkahun): you would marvel at its bad condition after you had witnessed it in its best state, or you would regret what you had toiled over and spent on, or regret the sins you had committed for its sake, and so you would converse about it. Tafakkuh (lit. "fruit-gathering") is the moving about among various kinds of fruit, and it has been used metaphorically for moving about in conversation.

It is also read as "tafakkanun" (تَفَكَّنُونَ), meaning: you would feel remorse. It is also read as "fazaltum" (فَظِلْتُمْ) with a kasra, and as "fazallatum" (فَظَلِلْتُمْ) in its original form.

Qur'an 56:66: ﴿Indeed, we are burdened with debt.﴾ That is: we are obligated to pay the cost of what we have spent, or we are destroyed, our provision having been ruined, from al-gharam (ruin), which means destruction. It is read "a-innā" (as an interrogative). In both readings, the sentence is governed by an implied saying, which is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the subject of "tafakkahūn" (you continue to be amazed): meaning, saying, or you say, "Indeed, we are burdened with debt."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 67:

﴿Nay, we are deprived.﴾ We have been deprived of our provision, or we are ruined (muhārafūn), cut off from fortune: we have no share and no luck (lā bakht), we are unlucky (majdūdūn).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 68:

﴿Have you then considered the water which you drink?﴾ [Sweet and fresh (ʿadhban furatan)]. The specifying of this attribute by mention, despite the abundance of its benefits, is because drinking is the most important of the purposes connected with it.

﴿Is it you who sent it down from the clouds (al-muzn)?﴾ That is, from the clouds (al-sahab). Its singular is muznah. It was also said: it is the white cloud, and its water is sweeter.

﴿Or are We the ones who send it down?﴾ By Our power.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 70:

﴿Had We willed, We would have made it salty (ujaj)﴾, meaning brackish and bitter, such that it cannot be drunk. The omission of the lam (the particle of emphasis in the apodosis) here, while it is retained in the first conditional clause, is either because reliance is placed on the hearer's knowledge, or to distinguish between what is eaten and what is drunk in terms of importance and the difficulty of losing them. The two conditional clauses are resumptive (isti'nafiyyah), brought to show that His, exalted is He, preserving the crops and the water from whatever would spoil enjoyment of them is another blessing, after the blessing of causing growth and sending down, and one that calls for gratitude. Therefore His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Will you not then give thanks?﴾ is an exhortation (tahdid) to give thanks for all of it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 71:

﴿Have you then considered the fire which you kindle?﴾ That is: which you strike and extract from the firestick (zind).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 72:

﴿Have you brought into being its tree?﴾ — the one from which the firestarter is made, namely the markh and the 'afar.

﴿Or are We the producers?﴾ — of it, by Our power. The expression of its creation by "bringing into being" (insha') indicates the wondrous craftsmanship and expresses the perfection of power and wisdom, because of the strangeness in it that distinguishes it from all other trees, which are not free of fire, to the point that it is said that in every tree there is fire, and the markh and the 'afar are the most famous for it. Likewise, the expression of the breathing of the spirit as "bringing into being" is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We brought him into being as another creation﴾, for this same reason.(p-199)

The commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 73:

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We made it a reminder and a provision for the desert-dwellers﴾

His saying ﴿We made it a reminder﴾ is a resumptive clause (istiʾnaf) explaining its benefits, meaning: We made it a reminder of the Fire of Hell, in that We set in it the means of livelihood so that they would look at it and remember what they were promised of the Fire of Hell. Or it is a reminder and a model (unmudhaj) of the Fire of Hell, in accordance with what has been narrated from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "Your fire which the children of Adam kindle is one part of seventy parts of the heat of Hell." It has also been said: it is a means of insight (tabsira) regarding the matter of resurrection, for it is no more wondrous than bringing fire out of the moist wood.

﴿And a provision﴾, meaning a benefit.

﴿For the desert-dwellers﴾ (al-muqwin): those who go down to the qiwa', which is the barren wilderness. Their being singled out for this is because they are most in need of it, for those who reside or who dwell near them are not compelled to strike the flint (iqtidah bil-zinad). It has also been permitted that by al-muqwin is meant those whose bellies and saddlebags have become empty of food, but this is far-fetched, because what concerns them and fills their need is not restricted to what is eaten only after cooking. The delay in mentioning this benefit is to alert that the more important is the otherworldly benefit.

The fa' (فَ) in His words, exalted is He, ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ marks the sequence of what follows from what has been enumerated of His wondrous creation and marvelous blessings. These blessings call for glorifying Him (tasbih, declaring Him exalted above all imperfection), exalted is He. The glorification may be a declaration of His transcendence (tanzih, declaring Him free of what is unfitting) above what those who deny His oneness and disbelieve in His blessing, despite their greatness and abundance, say. It may be an expression of wonder at their disregard of those dazzling blessings, despite their great worth and evident manifestation. Or it may be thanks for those past blessings. That is: begin the glorification by mentioning His name, exalted is He, or by mentioning Him, since applying a name to a thing is a mention of it. The word al-'Azim (الْعَظِيمُ) is an adjective of either the name (الِاسْمِ) or the Lord (الرَّبِّ).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 75:

﴿Then I swear not﴾ means: "Then I swear." The "lā" is an emphatic addition, as in His saying, ﴿so that not﴾ (Qur'an 57:29). Or it is "fa-la-anā uqsimu," where the subject has been omitted and the fatḥa of the lām of initiation (lām al-ibtidāʾ) has been lengthened. This is supported by the reading of one who recited "fa-l-uqsim" (so, let me swear). Or it means "fa-lā rādda li-kalāmin yukhālifu al-muqsamu ʿalayhi" (so there is no rejecting of a statement that contradicts what is sworn to). As for what has been said about the meaning being "fa-lā uqsimu" (I do not swear), since the matter is too clear to need an oath, this is rejected by the specification of what is sworn by and the magnification of the matter of the oath by it.

﴿by the positions of the stars﴾ means: by their setting places, which are their places of setting. Their being specified for the oath is due to the disappearance of their traces in their setting, and to indicating the existence of a permanent influence that does not change; or because that is the time when those who pray at night and those who humbly supplicate to Him, exalted is He, stand, and the time when mercy and approval descend upon them. Or it means by their stations and courses, for in that there is, for Him, exalted is He, evidence of the greatness of His power and the perfection of His wisdom that expression cannot encompass. It was also said: "the stars" means the stars of the Qur'an, and "their positions" means the times of their revelation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 76:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed it is a mighty oath, if you only knew﴾ is an interjection within an interjection (i'tiraD), intended to emphasize and reinforce the content of the oath-clause. He interposed the words ﴿And indeed it is a mighty oath﴾ between the oath and its answer, which is His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 77:

﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾ (p-200) That is: abundant in benefit, due to its containing the fundamental sciences that are important for the welfare of this life and the Hereafter; or good and well-pleasing; or noble in the sight of Allah the Exalted. By His saying, the Exalted: ﴿if you knew﴾, [the phrase] comes between the described (al-mawsuf) and its description (sifah). The answer to "law" (lau, "if") is either omitted, intending by it the negation of their knowledge, or it is deleted, relying on its being evident, i.e.: you would have glorified it, or you would have acted in accordance with its requirements.

Translation:

﴿In a Book well-guarded﴾: i.e., protected from anyone other than the angels brought near (to God), so that none besides them can gain access to it; and it is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 79:

﴿None touches it except the purified﴾. Either this is another attribute of "a Book" (kitab), in which case "the purified" (al-mutahharun) refers to the angels, who are exalted above bodily impurities and the defilements of sins; or it is an attribute of the Qur'an, in which case "the purified" refers to those purified from ritual impurities (ahdath). In that case it is a negation with the meaning of a prohibition, i.e., it is not fitting that it be touched except by one who is in a state of purity (taharah) from among people, following the manner of his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "The Muslim is the brother of the Muslim: he does not wrong him, nor does he abandon him," meaning: it is not fitting for him to wrong him. It has also been said: it is not sought except by those purified from disbelief (kufr).

It was read as "al-mutatahhirun" and "al-muttahhirun" (with idgham, assimilation of the taʾ into the ṭaʾ), and as "al-muhtahirun"... [sic] — more precisely, "al-muthahhirun" from athharahu, meaning "tahharahu" (to purify), and "al-mutahhirun", i.e., purifying themselves or others through seeking forgiveness (istighfar) or otherwise.

﴿A revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ is another attribute of "the Qur'an." It is a verbal noun (masdar) used as an attribute, to the point that it took the place of its name. It is also read as "tanzilan."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 81:

﴿Is it then at this discourse﴾ which has been described with its sublime attributes that necessitate its glorification and reverence, namely the Noble Qur'an?

﴿That you are disdainful?﴾ That is, you are treating it lightly, like one who is "mudhin" (yudhinu) in a matter, meaning he softens his side toward it and does not stand firm in it, out of contempt for it.

And you make your provision [the thanks for your provision]: i.e., the thanks for your provision.

﴿that you deny﴾: i.e., you place denial in the place of thanks. It is also read "and you make your thanks [that] you deny," i.e., you make your thanks for the blessing of the Qur'an to be that you deny it. It has also been said: the provision is the rain, and the meaning is: you make the thanks for what Allah the Exalted provides you of rain [to be] that you deny that it comes from Allah the Exalted, in that you attribute it to the stars (anwa'). The first interpretation, however, is more in keeping with the context (siyaq) and the flow (sibaq) of this noble arrangement of verses.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 83:

Indeed, His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Why then, when it reaches the throat﴾ ... etc., is a rebuke founded upon their denial of the Qur'an in what His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We created you﴾ up to here, spoke of, from the striking verses that indicate that they are under His dominion (malakut), exalted is He, both as to their own essences and as to their food and drink and all the other means of their livelihood, as you will be made to see. And "lawla" (why not) is for urging (tahdid), to make their helplessness manifest, and "idha" (when) is temporal, meaning: why not, when the soul (nafs), i.e., the spirit (ruh), reaches the throat, and it has been said: (p-201) the soul of the throat, and it hastens toward departure.

﴿And you, at that moment﴾ O you who are present around the dying person.

﴿are looking on﴾ at what he is undergoing of the agonies of death.

We are closer to him (in knowledge, power and control) than you are, but you do not see.

Translation:

﴿And We are closer to him﴾ in knowledge, power and control.

﴿than you are﴾, for you do not know of his state except what you witness of the signs of the agony, without being able to grasp its reality, its manner and its causes, nor being able to repel even the least part of it. And We are the ones who take charge of the details of his condition, by Our knowledge and Our power, or through the angels of death.

﴿But you do not see﴾, meaning you do not perceive that, because of your ignorance of Our affairs.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then why not, if you are not subject to being judged?﴾ That is: not owned or governed (مَرْبُوبِينَ), from "dāna al-sultān ra'iyyatahu" (the ruler subjugated his subjects), when he governs them and makes them servants, looking to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We created you, so why do you not believe?﴾ For the tahdid (rebuke urging a course of action) necessarily presupposes that what is urged upon is absent.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 87:

And His saying, ﴿you return it﴾, meaning: the soul to its place, is the governing element of "idhā" (when), and the one being urged upon by "lawlā" (why not) the first time. The second is repeated for emphasis, and it, together with what is within its scope, is the indication of the response of the conditional clause. The meaning is: if you are not ones who are made to be lords (not created and subject to a Lord), as its indication is your not affirming Our creating you, then why do you not return the soul to its place when it reaches the throat (al-ḥulqūm)?

﴿If you are truthful﴾ in your belief. For their not affirming His being the Creator is an expression of their affirming that He, exalted is He, is not the Creator, according to the requirement of their doctrine.

Its statement, the Exalted: ﴿Then, if he is among those brought near﴾ ... etc. is the beginning of explaining the condition of the deceased after death, following the explanation of his condition at the time of death. That is: "Then, if he who was described is among the foremost of the three kinds, they are expressed by their most exalted attributes."

﴿Then rest﴾, meaning he has repose (istirāḥah). It is also read as "فَرُوحٌ" with a ḍammah on the rāʾ, and it has been explained as mercy, because mercy is the cause of the life of the one who receives it, and as everlasting life.

﴿And sweet basil﴾, meaning and provision (rizq).

﴿And gardens of delight﴾, meaning possessing delight (dhāt tanaʿum).

Verse 90: ﴿And as for if he is among the companions of the right hand﴾. He refers to them by the title already mentioned, since no single descriptive attribute had been given for them previously that would indicate their status other than this, as was mentioned for the other two groups.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim), on surah 56, verse 91:

(p-202) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Peace be upon you from the companions of the right hand﴾ is a report from Him, exalted is He, of some of them greeting others with peace, as the lam (the preposition "to/for") makes clear. It is not a quotation of the act of uttering peace by some of them toward others; for otherwise it would have said "upon you" (ʿalayka). The shift to addressing each one of them individually is for honor.

Qur'an 56:92: "But as for if he is of the deniers, the astray,"—and they are the people of the left. He referred to them by this description, just as they were described when their states were explained, in His saying, Exalted is He: "Then indeed you, O astray ones, deniers," as a censure of them by it and an indication of the cause of the punishment with which they were afflicted.
﴿Fa-nuzulun﴾ means: then for him there is a welcome-feast (nuzul) consisting of ﴿boiling water (hamim)﴾, which is drunk after eating the zaqqum, as was detailed earlier.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 56, verse 94:

﴿And burning in Hellfire﴾. That is: entry into the Fire. It has also been said: it means remaining in it and suffering its various kinds of punishment. And it has been said: that is what he finds in the grave of the scorching winds of the Fire and its smoke.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (*Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim*) on Surah 56, verse 95:

﴿Indeed, this﴾: that is, that which has been mentioned in this noble surah.

﴿Indeed, it is the truth of certainty﴾: that is, the truth of the certain report. It has also been said: the established truth of certainty.

The fa' in His words, ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾, is for the sequencing of the glorification, or of the command to it, upon what precedes it. For the truth of what has been detailed within this noble surah, of what necessitates His exaltation above what does not befit His majestic station, among which is associating partners with Him and denying His signs that speak the truth, [is established].

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Waqi'ah every night, poverty will never afflict him."
